Cross-validation folds that follow the data's structure

Source: R/ilm_folds.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_folds.Rd

Splits the rows of data into training and test sets for cross-validation. The folds are row indices, so they can be inspected, and reused for every model being compared: two models scored on the same folds can be compared fold by fold.

Usage

ilm_folds(
  data,
  type = c("random", "grouped", "blocked", "rolling"),
  K = 5L,
  group = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  initial = NULL,
  horizon = 1L,
  step = 1L,
  window = c("expanding", "sliding"),
  size = NULL,
  gap = 0L,
  known = NULL,
  seed = 1L
)

Arguments

data

A data frame: the rows the models are fitted to.

type

The kind of fold; see Which kind of fold.

K

Number of folds, for random, grouped and blocked folds.

group

For grouped folds, the name of the grouping column in data.

time

For blocked and rolling folds, the name of the time column in data: numeric, a Date or a date-time.

initial

For rolling folds, the number of time points in the first training window.

horizon

For rolling folds, the number of time points in each test set.

step

For rolling folds, how many time points the origin moves from one fold to the next.

window

For rolling folds: "expanding" trains on every time point up to the origin, "sliding" on the last size of them.

size

For a sliding window, the number of time points it trains on. Defaults to initial.

gap

Time points left out between training and test rows: after the origin for rolling folds, and on both sides of the test block for blocked folds.

known

For rolling folds, the names of the covariates whose future values would be known at the origin; see Ex-ante and ex-post.

seed

Seed for random and grouped folds. The caller's random-number state is restored afterwards.

Value

An object of class "ilm_folds": a list with one element per fold, each holding train and test row indices, and for rolling folds the fold's origin and each test row's horizon. as.data.frame() gives one row per data row and fold.

Which kind of fold

The folds decide which question the cross-validation answers, so they should match the prediction being made.

  • "random": rows are held out at random. Every held-out row's group is still in the training data, so this scores predictions for units the model has seen. On data with a time structure it scores interpolation, not forecasting.

  • "grouped": whole groups are held out together, so this scores predictions for new units. Random folds would overstate how well a model predicts a unit it has never seen.

  • "blocked": contiguous blocks of time are held out, optionally with a gap either side so that rows next to the block do not leak into training.

  • "rolling": rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation. Each fold trains on the times up to an origin and tests on the horizon times after it, so every test row is a genuine forecast. For a model with an autoregressive term, this is the scheme that scores forecasts. Random and blocked folds let the model see both sides of a held-out time, so they score interpolation and overstate forecast skill.

Rolling origins are the reference's "evaluation on a rolling forecasting origin": every training set holds only rows before its test rows, and the scores are averaged over the test sets. Which question each of the other kinds answers is limn's own reasoning.

Time points and horizons

Blocked and rolling folds count time points: the distinct values of time in data, in order. Every row at a time point goes into the same set, so a panel of several series is split at the same times for all of them. A test row's horizon is how many time points after the origin it lies, so with gap = 0 the first test time point has horizon 1.

Ex-ante and ex-post

A forecast is ex-ante when it uses only what would have been known at the origin. Covariates the model uses at their realised future values, such as the weather on the day being forecast, make it ex-post, and flatter the forecast. Name in known the covariates whose future values would genuinely be known, such as a calendar or a planned dose. The folds record it so the evaluation can say which kind it is.

References

Hyndman, R. J. and Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition. OTexts. Section 5.10, "Time series cross-validation" (online edition, https://otexts.com/fpp3/toolbox.html#sec-tscv, read 27 October 2026).

See also

ilm_cv(), which scores a model on the folds; ilm_compare(), which compares two models' scores on the same folds.

Examples

d <- data.frame(site = rep(letters[1:6], each = 8), month = rep(1:8, 6),
                y = rnorm(48))
ilm_folds(d, "grouped", K = 3, group = "site")
#> <ilm_folds> 3 grouped folds (whole groups of 'site' held out)
#>   48 rows; training rows 32, test rows 16 per fold
f <- ilm_folds(d, "rolling", time = "month", initial = 5, horizon = 2)
f
#> <ilm_folds> 2 rolling origins over time ('month'), expanding window
#>   48 rows; training rows 30 to 36, test rows 12 per fold
#>   first origin after 5 time points, then every 1
#>   horizons 1 to 2
#>   known in advance: none named, so any covariate makes the evaluation ex-post
head(as.data.frame(f))
#>   fold row   set origin horizon
#> 1    1   1 train      5      NA
#> 2    1   2 train      5      NA
#> 3    1   3 train      5      NA
#> 4    1   4 train      5      NA
#> 5    1   5 train      5      NA
#> 6    1   9 train      5      NA
